analysis.one_liner: Bars members of Congress, their spouses, and young children from owning individual stocks or similar investments, requiring divestiture or blind trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require members of Congress, along with their spouses and children under 19, to sell off or place in a blind trust any individual stocks, commodities, futures, or similar investments. Members could keep broad index funds, Treasury bonds, and government retirement plans. Anyone who failed to comply would owe a fine equal to one month's congressional salary, charged every 30 days until fixed. The bill was introduced in September 2023 with eight Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The public benefits from reduced conflicts of interest: lawmakers could no longer trade stocks in industries they regulate or vote on, and could not keep those holdings in their spouse's or young child's name to get around it. Members who currently profit from well-timed trades would lose that option, as the rules cover direct holdings, investments through funds and trusts, and derivative workarounds like options [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and public trust in Congress

how_it_helps.text: It removes the conflict of interest created when lawmakers vote on legislation while they, their spouses, or young children own individual stocks, commodities, futures, or derivative-style stakes in the industries being regulated.
Compliance documents, trust schedules, extensions, and penalties must be posted publicly, making it easy for anyone to check whether a member complied.
The rules apply for the whole period of service plus 180 days after leaving, closing the revolving window in which a departing member could still trade on inside knowledge.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who would have to divest or blind-trust individual securities, commodities, futures, and derivatives for their entire time in office plus 180 days after. They would bear the cost of setting up approved blind trusts and, for non-compliance, a fine equal to one month's salary repeated every 30 days [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress with stock holdings

drawbacks.text: A blind trust is not a perfect shield: the lawmaker still knows which assets were placed in it, so divestiture is the stronger remedy, and members could choose the trust route rather than selling.
The penalty — a fine equal to one month's salary, repeated monthly — is real but modest for the wealthiest members, and enforcement rests on ethics offices rather than criminal penalties.
Members would bear the administrative cost of setting up approved blind trusts and could face tax friction from forced divestiture, which is the strongest good-faith objection raised to such bans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be removing a direct conflict of interest between lawmakers' personal finances and their legislative duties; the cost is minimal for the public, though lawmakers would lose the ability to manage their own investments and would bear trust-administration and divestiture costs. Honest objections: a blind trust is imperfect (the lawmaker knows what was placed in it), the penalty is small relative to some members' wealth, and enforcement depends on the ethics offices. Still, the bill is far stronger than the current disclosure-only regime. The bigger weakness is that it never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security Committee in September 2023, and the committee never voted on it or reported it out before the two-year Congress ended in January 2025, so it died without any floor vote.

narrative.text: Ossoff introduced the bill on September 12, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
The complete action history shows only the introduction and committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not passed by both chambers die at the end of a Congress.
Eight Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who hold or trade individual stocks keep that ability; no ethics rules changed. The status quo, governed only by disclosure rules, continues.

for.name: Sen. Jon Ossoff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ban Congressional Stock Trading Act on September 12, 2023.

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Kelly, Warnock, Bennet, Duckworth, Lujan, Schatz, Baldwin, Shaheen)

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a markup or reported it out, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Senate leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill or any congressional stock-trading ban for a Senate floor vote during the 118th Congress, despite multiple competing proposals from both parties.

sides.party_line_note: All eight cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding 49 Senate seats, the bill as introduced had no visible GOP support, though stock-trading bans in general drew interest from members of both parties.

industries.industry: Members of Congress with individual stock holdings
industries.note: Sitting lawmakers and their spouses would have to sell or blind-trust individual securities, commodities, futures, and derivatives during service, ending a form of personal investing that has been profitable for some members.
The bill explicitly leaves diversified index funds and ETFs allowed, so ordinary-style broad-market investing by lawmakers continues; the industry loses nothing.
Some individual stock trading by a small group of wealthy households (members and spouses) would end, which is a negligible business effect; brokerages lose a few hundred accounts at most.
